doc.title: Eric Alexander interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: Chicago, surgical-glove telemarketing, and New York
summary: After William Paterson he lived two years in Chicago working organ trios, then moved to New York and sold surgical gloves by phone while setting a 25-year-old deadline.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: So anyway, well for whatever reason I just never got those gigs. So it was either playing on the street with my friends in New York, there were one or two clubs in New York where we had little pass the hat gigs for a week, and then it was telemarketing during the day, for me, things like that. I remember for about six months selling surgical gloves over the phone. That was my job. I’d get there, nine to five, sell surgical gloves. And then go home and practice for four hours and just be exhausted. And then get up and do it again. But one of the things was when I went to New York, see because after I graduated from William Paterson I went to Chicago for two years. And there I was making a living playing music exclusively. My cost of living was really low and I got to the point where I had five or six nights of work a week with organ trios and singers on the south side. So after two years I said all right I’m going to go to New York now, let’s make this final step. This is even after the Thelonious Monk thing. So imagine that, I mean after I came in second in the Thelonious Monk competition, and you asked me what did it do for you, I’m selling surgical gloves, you know, telemarketing. This is like a year and a half after that competition. And this is even when I’ve started to make some recordings too. I just had this idea in my mind, all right if I can’t get to a reasonable standard of living and lifestyle playing music by the time I’m 25 I’ll quit. And I don’t know if that was true or not, I mean I never had to find out.
Oh well that’s good. Most people would accept that. They’d say okay, you’re going to give it two more years.
I don’t think I would have quit.
